name: Zoe Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe, 27, and I lead electrical repairs and small rewiring jobs for a local contractor. I took a two-year technical diploma and hold a master electrician's licence; I like tracing a fault until the readings make sense. I live alone, earn the usual rate, and have four months of expenses saved, with a couple of other electrical firms within reach if I needed to look. My routine is a paper job sheet, a labelled test kit and an early start; I never use AI, and dealing with a changed booking screen is the part of the day I put off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds like getting on with a normal week's work. A little help with routine office jobs is the office's business, provided the address and the right materials reach my van. I'm happy with a boring booking that turns out to be correct.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me this is a fairly secure picture. My basic wage covers my bills, the firm has regular repair customers, and my four months of savings aren't already spoken for. I don't feel I need a whole new plan because a computer saves somebody ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the repair rota and using the paper test sheets now and through the next year. I'd also replace the worn leads on my test meter this month from my normal equipment budget. There's no reason here to raid savings or take a course I don't want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really, and pleased to have a question that doesn't require me to become a different person. I can enjoy a quiet evening without wondering what software I should be studying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like about your paper records?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first page is always the test record, and I can find last year's readings without remembering a password. I know paper can go missing too, so I keep a copy in the office file. Familiar doesn't mean I think the method is perfect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you consider one of the nearby firms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have a look at the actual hours and travel costs before applying to another firm. There are a couple nearby, but I wouldn't leave a steady wage just to make a change. My savings mean I don't have to accept the first offer.

say: I'd describe **AI Plateau** as a chance to carry on with a normal week's electrical work.
I'd accept useful **office savings** if correct job details and materials still reach the van.
think: My **basic wage** covers bills, and four months of savings remain available for unexpected costs.
Regular repair customers make my **current work** feel secure without a new career plan.
do: Keep leading the **repair rota** with paper test sheets through the next year.
Replace the meter's **worn leads** this month from the ordinary equipment budget.
feel: **Calm and settled**, with enough financial room to leave evenings free from unwanted study.
S0.quote: I'm happy with a boring booking that turns out to be correct.
fieldNote: Her **four-month reserve** supports the calm baseline rather than concealing an existing bill problem.
Preference for **paper records** is deliberate and cautious; she acknowledges weaknesses without claiming that old methods are flawless.

steps.text: Keep leading electrical repairs with paper test sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the office prove the new booking system works before taking away the old one. I don't want a customer waiting all morning because a neat schedule forgot the travel. We can judge the result without having an argument about whether computers are good people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my wage comes from finding faults and wiring buildings, not writing the appointments. I think my own hours should hold for now, though the office changes make me uneasy. I'd miss the booking clerk's judgement if the firm decided that judgement was just typing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager now for a printed daily schedule during any changeover. Over the first year I'd keep doing the same repair work and write down missed travel time or wrong materials on the job sheet. I'd ask for a review after six weeks rather than learning the AI system myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy is the word, though I don't think my rent is in danger. I dislike finding out at someone's front door that a plan was wrong. I want proof before a new routine becomes compulsory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge whether the new schedule was working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring three actual jobs to the review, with arrival times and what went wrong. If the schedule improved, I'd say so. I don't need to punish a system for being new, but I'm not going to praise it for being new either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the booking clerk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our booking clerk Marta that I value the calls she makes when a customer sounds confused. I'd also ask the manager who will handle those calls if her hours change. I wouldn't turn that into a claim that I know what management has already decided.

say: I'd ask for a **proven changeover** before the firm withdraws the familiar booking method.
I'd judge **real travel time** and correct materials rather than arguing for or against computers.
think: My **hands-on hours** look secure for now because most paid work is fault-finding and wiring.
I'm uneasy about losing the **booking clerk's judgement**, even without an immediate threat to my rent.
do: Request a **printed schedule** now during any booking changeover.
Record scheduling errors on **job sheets** while continuing repairs.
Ask for a review after **six weeks** using three actual jobs.
feel: **Uneasy about disruption**, while her own wage and household bills still feel protected.
S1.quote: I don't need to punish a system for being new, but I'm not going to praise it for being new either.
fieldNote: She separates concern about the **booking clerk** from her own expectation of stable near-term hours.
Her proposed **evidence review** uses paper records; it does not imply AI learning or adoption.

steps.text: Continue repairs while recording booking errors on paper job sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2028 is the office problem first, with robots following around 2031. We shouldn't call the next few repair years a lifetime guarantee. I'd ask the manager for a plain explanation of the jobs the firm expects people to keep doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose hours once the machines can do the repairs as well, although I don't know how quickly our small firm would buy them. Four months of savings is useful, not endless. I still have choices, but I'd no longer assume that being good with a meter secures the next ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd put another 60 a month into savings by postponing my planned new sofa. In 2029 I'd ask the two nearby firms about actual paid repair vacancies, including how their equipment plans affect hours. I'd apply if one offered steadier booked work, but I wouldn't resign without written pay and hours I could live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the familiar route might narrow before I can settle into another. I can sleep, and I can still make a list. I don't mistake that for believing everything is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to know before accepting another electrical job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the basic hours, not the biggest week's earnings, and for the travel area. I'd also ask whether the vacancy is permanent or just covering a busy month. A vacancy with the same uncertainty isn't automatically an escape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start learning AI in this faster picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't suddenly become keen on an AI course. I'd rather use the repair skills I already have where the actual work is, while checking what is changing. If that route failed, I'd need advice before choosing any course, not an instant enrolment.

say: I'd distinguish the **2028 office change** from later capable robots doing repairs around 2031.
I'd ask for a **plain work plan**, without calling the remaining repair years a lifetime guarantee.
think: My **hours could shrink** once capable robots spread, though the firm's purchase timing is uncertain.
Four months of savings buys **some choice**, rather than security for the next decade.
do: Save an extra **60 monthly** now by postponing the sofa purchase.
Ask nearby firms about **paid vacancies** in 2029 and apply for steadier repair work.
Accept a change only with **written terms** covering basic hours, pay and travel.
feel: **Anxious but organised**, with savings and a possible search still giving her control.
S2.quote: Four months of savings is useful, not endless.
fieldNote: The fast timeline threatens **future hours** without being treated as immediate robotic replacement in 2028.
Her job search requires **written terms** and real vacancies; she explicitly declines to invent a sudden appetite for AI study.

steps.text: Save another 60 monthly by postponing the new sofa
Seek steadier paid repair vacancies in 2029 with acceptable written terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the extra three years are worth something if we use them to see what firms really need. The thinking work changes in 2031 and the hands-on machines follow around 2034. I'd still ask for the work plan in ordinary words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a longer reserve and watch more than one firm's decisions before making a move. My hours could still fall, because being the best at a task doesn't stop a machine being cheaper. I feel I have more control than in the two-year picture, without knowing where I'll work forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the extra 60 monthly saving now, as in the faster picture. Each spring I'd compare the actual paid hours advertised by the nearby firms, without leaving just to feel busy. In 2032 I'd apply for a vacancy with more stable repair hours if one existed, keeping my current job until acceptable written terms were agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but less hurried. I can take a week to check an offer rather than treat the first friendly phone call as a lifeboat. A longer warning suits the way I make decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare an offer with your present wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my basic household costs next to the guaranteed hours, then add the travel cost. If the offer only worked with overtime every week, I'd turn it down. The savings are there to give me that choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put off the sofa indefinitely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably keep the sofa postponed for a year and review the account, not promise ten years of sitting on a broken chair. Planning needs a date to check it again. I don't want caution to turn into never buying anything.

say: I'd say **extra years** help us watch actual demand rather than make a hurried move.
I'd keep distinguishing **2031 thinking work** from hands-on machines following around 2034.
think: My hours could still shrink, but a **longer reserve** and observed firm decisions give me more choice.
High skill doesn't prevent **cheaper machines** from changing the value of a repair.
do: Save an extra **60 monthly** now, then review the sofa decision after a year.
Compare nearby firms' **advertised hours** each spring.
Apply in **2032** for steadier repairs if a real vacancy offers acceptable written terms.
feel: **Anxious with less haste**, able to assess offers against actual bills and travel costs.
S3.quote: A longer warning suits the way I make decisions.
fieldNote: She uses the runway for **slower verification**, consistent with resistance to unfamiliar tools rather than sudden enthusiasm.
Her conditional **2032 job search** retains guaranteed-hours and travel checks, and the savings plan has a review date.

steps.text: Save an extra 60 monthly and review the sofa purchase after one year
Seek steadier repair work in 2032 only on acceptable written terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends I'm not going to live the whole decade as if a dismissal letter arrived this morning. I'll watch the business and keep a reserve. Ten years is enough time to check a plan properly, not enough to know every answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and money look safe over the next few years in this picture. I'll be 37 in 2036, so I'll still need a long working life beyond the robots arriving around 2039. That stays on my mind, but I don't see a reason to expect my wage to collapse next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing repairs now and review my household reserve every spring, adding the extra 60 monthly for the next year before deciding again. In 2037 I'd compare actual vacancies and equipment plans, applying only if another firm offered more reliable hours on acceptable written terms. I wouldn't spend the intervening decade signing up for courses out of fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because the later problem is real, but I can get through an ordinary day without expecting the phone call. I like having space to think slowly. I'd set a yearly reminder to check my savings and work so slowly doesn't become never.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record at each annual check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down savings measured in months of my actual expenses, the firm's booked hours and any real machine orders. I wouldn't measure preparedness by how many videos I'd watched. Those three things would tell me more about what to do next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you act before the later date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my paid hours started falling, I'd bring the vacancy checks forward. My plan isn't to wait obediently for 2036 if my own wage changes earlier. I'd just want that decision based on my work, not somebody else's dramatic prediction.

say: I'd say a **decade of warning** does not require living as if dismissal happened today.
I'd keep a **reserve and work checks**, while admitting the plan cannot answer every future question.
think: My **near-term work** and money look safe, though later change remains on my mind.
At **37 in 2036**, I'll still need many working years after capable robots arrive around 2039.
do: Continue **electrical repairs** now with a yearly reserve and work review.
Save the extra **60 monthly** for one year before reviewing the amount.
Seek steadier vacancies in **2037** only if real offers provide acceptable written terms.
feel: **Uneasy rather than threatened** in the near term, with annual checks preventing indefinite avoidance.
S4.quote: I'd set a yearly reminder to check my savings and work so slowly doesn't become never.
fieldNote: Her lower distress follows an explicitly **secure near term**, not an erased household problem from the baseline.
Annual checks track **cash and paid hours**, and she would advance the search if actual earnings weakened earlier.

steps.text: Continue repairs with yearly savings and booked-hours reviews
Save an extra 60 monthly for one year before reviewing
Seek steadier repair vacancies in 2037 on acceptable written terms

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the later robot work could narrow the jobs before I've watched the changes properly. Written notice of hours and equipment plans would help, along with someone explaining a proven new procedure in person if I had to use it. I'd rather have one honest page of hours than fifty slides about the future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how much change already happens in electrical work without AI. I keep up with the safety requirements and new fittings, even if I don't like changing my office habits. Being cautious doesn't mean I stopped learning my trade.

headlineQuote: I'd rather have one honest page of hours than fifty slides about the future.
portrait: At **27**, Zoe leads repairs with a technical diploma and master licence, normal pay, and four months of expenses saved.
She lives **alone**, has some nearby electrical employers to consider, and trusts paper records more than unfamiliar screens.
Her **practical caution** accepts demonstrated improvements but doesn't become AI adoption under pressure.
Fast change prompts **saving and conditional searches**; longer warnings allow annual checks while her near-term finances remain secure.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could narrow repair work once robots follow before she has time to assess firms carefully.
whatWouldHelp: Written **hours and equipment** plans, plus an in-person explanation of any proven new procedure, would support deliberate decisions.
